titre: Churchill (1947): “The Worst Form of Government,” a Phrase He Reports
accroche: Before his most famous line on democracy, Churchill says “it has been said”: he reports it without claiming it.
contenu_vulgarise:
On November 11, 1947, the House of Commons debates a bill that reduces the powers of the House of Lords, the *Parliament Bill*. Winston Churchill, then Leader of the Opposition, takes the floor. In the middle of his speech, he utters a sentence that the whole world has attributed to him ever since: democracy is supposedly “the worst form of government, except for all the others.” It is generally cited as a personal thought, almost as his profession of faith. The official record of the debates says something else.

## What the Record Says

Hansard, which publishes the British parliamentary debates, reports the passage: “Many forms of Government have been tried, and will be tried in this world of sin and woe. No one pretends that democracy is perfect or all-wise. Indeed, it has been said that democracy is the worst form of Government except all those other forms that have been tried from time to time.” Two details matter. Churchill does not claim the phrase: he reports it (“it has been said”), without naming who said it. And he places it in a specific debate, that of the bill on the Lords, in which he opposes the reduction of the House of Lords' delaying power.

## A Reported Phrase

On the origin of the sentence, the entry's sources do not settle the matter. Hansard shows that Churchill presents it as something already said (“it has been said”), without naming anyone; the Churchill Society page reproduces only the quotation, with no comment on its origin, and no source consulted identifies an earlier author. All we know is that the version usually given is a shortcut: the original text is longer, more hesitant, and the turn “except for all the others” comes from a paragraph that begins by conceding that democracy is far from perfect.

## The Shift

The context shifts the meaning. In the text, the sentence comes after an admission: no one pretends that democracy is perfect or infallible. It sits inside a concession, not inside a demonstration of the regime's superiority over the others: Churchill goes on to evoke the feeling that the people should rule and that opinion should guide the ministers. What the isolated quotation presents as a doctrine is, in the record, an aside reported in passing in the course of a debate. A lesson of method remains: before citing a famous sentence, it pays to open the text that contains it, because the abridged version often loses the “it has been said” and the context that change its scope.

carte.punch: Churchill says “it has been said”: he reports the phrase.
carte.idee: On November 11, 1947, in the Commons, Churchill declares: “it has been said that democracy is the worst form of government, except for all the others.” He presents the phrase as something already said, without naming its author.

quiz.question: What does the Commons record of November 11, 1947, show about the phrase “the worst form of government”?
choix: Churchill invents it on the spot to conclude a speech devoted to the Cold War
Churchill reports it as something already said, without naming its author
Churchill signs it by citing it from a speech by Clemenceau
Churchill utters it to criticize democracy, which he judges inferior to other regimes
quiz.explication: Hansard has “it has been said”: Churchill reports the phrase without naming its author, and the date of the sitting is that of the Parliament Bill, not of a speech on the Cold War. The meaning is not critical: it is a concession.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which bill is the Commons debating on November 11, 1947, when Churchill utters this sentence?
choix: A law on the nationalization of the coal mines
A reform of the Commons electoral system
The Parliament Bill, which reduces the powers of the House of Lords
The peace treaty signed with Germany
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On November 11, 1947, the Commons debates the Parliament Bill, which reduces the delaying power of the House of Lords, and it is in this debate that Churchill utters the sentence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What role does Churchill hold in the Commons on the day he utters this sentence?
choix: Speaker of the House of Lords
A member with no portfolio or office
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In November 1947, Churchill is Leader of the Opposition: the Conservatives lost the 1945 elections, and he is neither prime minister nor speaker of the Lords.
